CausalChain: 3D scaffold formation -> Enhanced cell-cell and cell-ECM interactions & tight junction stabilization -> Activation of mechanotransductive pathways (Wnt/β-catenin, YAP/TAZ) -> Epigenetic modifications (increased histone acetylation, decreased DNA methylation) at CYP gene promoters -> Increased CYP expression and improved drug metabolism modeling
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that culturing HepG2 cells on a precisely engineered 3D scaffold will simultaneously enhance physical cell-cell interactions and induce robust tight junction formation as observed in low-density conditions, while also activating a spectrum of mechanotransductive pathways, including both Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ. This dual signaling will prompt specific epigenetic reprogramming at cytochrome P450 gene promoters—characterized by increased histone acetylation and reduced DNA methylation—thus restoring or enhancing CYP isoform expression. Utilizing advanced technologies such as high-content imaging, real-time PCR, and ChIP-seq, we aim to systematically validate each step of this cascade, thereby establishing a highly faithful HepG2 model for human hepatocyte drug metabolism.
Abstract: This study proposes that engineering a biomimetic three-dimensional (3D) scaffold, via advanced 3D bioprinting and microfabrication techniques, can recapitulate key features of native liver tissue by enhancing cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions. In this environment, HepG2 cells exhibit improved tight junction formation and polarized morphology, leading to the activation of mechanotransductive pathways, notably Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ. These pathways are hypothesized to trigger targeted epigenetic modifications—including histone acetylation and DNA demethylation—on cytochrome P450 (CYP) gene promoters. The net result is a restoration and enhancement of CYP expression, thereby improving the fidelity of HepG2 cells as in vitro models of human hepatocyte drug metabolism. This work leverages contemporary high-content imaging and chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) to systematically map the mechanotransductive and epigenetic changes induced by the 3D culture environment.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain of: (1) using a 3D scaffold to improve cell interactions and mechanical signaling; (2) activation of mechanotransductive pathways, originally focused on Wnt/β-catenin; (3) ensuing epigenetic reprogramming that restores CYP expression. However, it extends the original by integrating additional mechanosensitive factors such as YAP/TAZ and emphasizing the pivotal role of tight junction stabilization—illustrated by observations in low-density 2D cultures. Also, the revised hypothesis explicitly defines the type of epigenetic modifications (e.g., increased histone acetylation, decreased DNA methylation) and outlines practical techniques (3D bioprinting, high-content imaging, ChIP-seq) for validation, thereby enhancing both the mechanistic clarity and experimental feasibility compared to the original proposal.
